top_choice_rationale: P002 credits one specific, well-defined discovery: magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms in an optical lattice (Katori's concept, Ye's record-accuracy realisation to about 1e-18). It has been reproduced and intercompared at several laboratories and is already used for redshift tests and constraints on varying constants. Attribution is two names with a natural concept/demonstration split, and the citation can be written without the frequency comb or ion clocks, so it is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. P003 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, confined to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect and Z2) is a mature, well-confirmed second choice, though its credit is compound (Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Hasan) and adjacent to 2016. P001 is scientifically sound but the youngest case, with an open pairing mechanism and an unsettled Bistritzer/Andrei attribution, so I would revisit it later. An award is preferable to no award because all three proposals are sound.
recusal_note: No documented collaboration or institutional tie to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer; my profile-documented collaborators are not among the laureates. As a theoretical atomic physicist I am subject-area close to the clock case and may be biased toward it; not a recusal ground apparent from the profile.
